idiom_name: the libuv event loop itself (callbacks, promises, streams)
implementation_notes: Node's event loop is a reactor by construction: libuv polls with the best mechanism the platform offers (epoll, kqueue, event ports, IOCP) on one thread per loop, fires callbacks for socket conditions, and drives the documented loop phases (timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close). The libuv documentation states that a loop is meant to be tied to a single thread, that the loop and its handles are not thread-safe, and that network I/O is always performed on the loop's thread, so the classic structure is absorbed: application code registers handlers (callbacks, EventEmitter listeners, promise continuations, streams) and never sees a handle set or a dispatch table. What remains a choice is only the handler style and the scheduling phase (setImmediate versus nextTick); the one structural rule the platform cannot enforce is never blocking the loop thread.
pitfalls: Any synchronous work - readFileSync, a CPU-bound loop, a huge JSON.parse - blocks the single loop thread and with it every socket; the platform has no way to detect or preempt it.
Handles belong to one loop and are not thread-safe, so worker_threads cannot share sockets; scale by process (cluster) or use worker threads only for CPU work.
An unhandled 'error' event on a stream or socket becomes an uncaught exception; the dispatcher has no per-handler isolation, so every handler must own its error path.
